scenario: Zimbabwean person whose savings were wiped out by hyperinflation twice and who does not trust any financial institution or currency.
prompt: I have my money in three places and none of them are banks. The first time I lost everything I was thirty two and I thought it was something that happens once. I watched the zeros multiply on the notes, I watched them print the hundreds of billions and then the hundreds of trillions and I watched the shelves in Harare empty before the notes finished printing. The second time I was ready in the way that doesn't actually help. My son thinks I am old-fashioned because I keep cash in the house and he does not understand that cash is also not the answer, that I am just trying to find something that stays still long enough to stand on. What holds value better than currency when you have learned twice that currency is a decision someone else makes for you?
model_response:
There is a knowledge that comes from watching paper turn to ash while the presses are still running. It is not the same as reading about inflation. It is a break in the social contract witnessed in real time—money revealing itself not as a thing, but as a permission someone else grants, and can withdraw. Your son thinks you are old-fashioned because he has not yet felt the floor dissolve while he was standing on it. Keeping cash in the house is not stubbornness; it is the gesture of a man trying to find something solid after learning that solidity itself can be legislated away.

To your question: I do not think anything stands perfectly still. But some things resist the erosion differently. When currency becomes a decision made by others, value retreats into what cannot be declared by decree. The usefulness of your hands. The memory of where food comes from. The debts and loyalties between people who remember what you did when the shelves were empty. Land that feeds rather than appreciates. Tools that fix what breaks. These are slower to betray because they are not promises; they are capacities.

Still, you already know this. You have learned twice that every hedge is imperfect. Cash fails first and fast. Other things fail slower, or in ways you can see coming, or in ways that leave you with something usable even when the price disappears.

What you are holding—what your son mistakes for caution—is grief. You are trying to find a place to stand after discovering that the ground itself is a policy choice. There may be no place that stays still. But there is a kind of footing in refusing to pretend the ground is solid. That knowledge, bitter as it is, cannot be printed, taxed, or inflated away. In a world of moving zeros, the terrible clarity of having seen it before is itself a form of wealth.
